title: Cold-Smoked Muenster Cheese
summary: A monster block of Muenster, cut down and cold smoked overnight with pecan pellets below 50°F, then vacuum sealed to mellow.
article:
Cold weather means cold smoking. I picked up a monster block of Muenster from Restaurant Depot and turned it into a fridge full of smoked cheese, with plenty left over to give away.

## Why cut it down?

Smoke only flavors the surface, so smaller blocks mean more surface area and more smoke in every bite. I cut the big block into manageable pieces before it went in.

## Keep it cold

The whole trick to cold smoking is keeping the cheese below 50°F so it never sweats or melts. I lit two smoke tubes with Smokin' Pecan pellets, which add a deep, nutty aroma that pairs really well with cheese, and ran a fan to keep the temperature down. It smoked for about six hours and then sat in the smoker overnight, with the ambient temperature down around 35°F. If it's not that cold where you are, move it to the fridge, uncovered, for the night.

## Let it mellow

Freshly smoked cheese tastes harsh and ashy. I vacuum sealed some blocks whole and cubed up a few more. Let them mellow for at least one to two weeks before you dig in. The cubes make great holiday gifts.

items: 1 large block Muenster cheese (any size; I used a deli-sized block)
A small fan, if needed to keep the temperature down

steps: Cut the cheese into manageable blocks, about 2 inches thick, to increase the surface area for smoke.
Let the cheese sit out for 30 minutes so a little surface moisture evaporates, and pat dry.
Fill and light two smoke tubes with pecan pellets and set them in a smoker that's turned off.
Arrange the cheese on the grates with space between the blocks.
Smoke for about 6 hours, using a fan if needed to keep the chamber below 50°F.
Leave the cheese in the smoker overnight if it's cold enough outside (around 35°F). Otherwise, refrigerate uncovered.
Vacuum seal the blocks whole or cubed.
Refrigerate for at least 1–2 weeks to let the smoke mellow before eating.
notes: Pecan is mild and nutty. Apple and cherry are good alternatives for cheese.
This method works for gouda, cheddar and pepper jack too.
yield_text: As much cheese as you smoke
review_notes: Nearly everything is from your caption and on-screen text. The 2-inch block size and 30-minute surface dry are filled in.

title: Cheddar Poblano Beef & Pork Smoked Sausage
summary: My first homemade smoked sausage: beef, pork, poblano and sharp cheddar. Great flavor and that perfect snap, plus what I'd fix next time.
article:
My first time making sausage! The flavor was great and the casing had that perfect snap, but I'll be honest: the texture came out grainy and dry. I'm sharing the whole recipe anyway, along with what I learned, because that's half the fun of a new project.

## The recipe

Equal parts pork and beef, roasted poblano, a block of sharp cheddar, and Meat Church Gospel as the seasoning base. Curing salt makes it safe to cold smoke, potato starch helps hold it together, and a little water helps with mixing. I cured the links overnight and then cold smoked them for five hours.

## What went wrong

Partway through, the smoker had an unexpected temperature spike to 250°F before I got it back down to 225°F to finish. That spike probably rendered out a lot of fat. Sausage should come up to temperature gently, and high heat breaks the fat out of the meat.

Here are the lessons I put on screen for next time:

- Not enough salt. Aim for about 2% of the meat weight.
- Use ice water, and less of it.
- Mix more, and keep everything cold the whole time. A good long mix is what binds the proteins and gives sausage its snappy, juicy texture.

If you're an experienced sausage maker, I'd love your feedback. Follow along as I work on perfecting this one.

items: 2 poblano peppers, roasted, peeled and diced
90 g Meat Church The Gospel rub
8 oz ice water (next time: about half that)
1 block (8 oz) sharp cheddar, cut into small cubes

steps: Put the cubed meat and your grinder parts in the freezer until the meat is firm at the edges, 30–45 minutes.
Grind the pork and beef through a medium plate into a bowl set over ice.
Add the curing salt, potato starch, Gospel and ice water. Mix by hand or with a mixer paddle until the mixture turns sticky and tacky, 3–5 minutes. Keep it cold.
Fold in the poblanos and cheddar.
Stuff into casings and twist into links. Prick any air pockets.
Refrigerate the links uncovered overnight to cure and dry.
Cold smoke for about 5 hours.
Raise the smoker gradually to 160–175°F and cook until the sausage reaches 155–160°F internal. Avoid big temperature swings.
Plunge into an ice bath to stop the cooking and tighten the casings, then pat dry.
notes: Lessons from my first batch: aim for about 2% salt by meat weight, use ice water and less of it, and mix longer while keeping everything cold.
My temperature spike to 250°F likely caused the grainy texture. Go low and slow.
USDA recommends 160°F internal for ground beef and pork.
review_notes: Ingredient amounts, overnight cure, 5-hour cold smoke, the 250°F spike and the three on-screen lessons are from your caption and video. The grind and mix method, the gentle finish (160–175°F smoker to 155–160°F internal), the ice bath and the pecan wood are filled in.

title: Cold-Smoked Beef Belly Pastrami Bacon
summary: Beef belly cured like pastrami and cold smoked on a cool rainy day with pecan pellets. Slice it, cook it like bacon, and build the best BLT you've ever had.
article:
When the weather turns cool and rainy, I break out the pecan pellets and smoke tube. This one combines two of my favorite things: pastrami and bacon.

## Cure, rub, cold smoke

The beef belly gets the same cure as my pastrami, then a coat of pastrami rub. Instead of cooking it in the smoker, it's cold smoked: a smoke tube full of pecan pellets in a smoker that's turned off, on a cool day. The meat takes on deep smoke flavor without cooking, so it stays raw like store-bought bacon.

## Slice and cook to taste

Slice it thin or thick and cook it however you like. I like it seared over a hot fire until the edges crisp. Then I made a quick BLT for lunch with toasted bread, crisp lettuce and fresh tomato. Unreal.

Because it's cold smoked, this bacon is raw. Always cook it before eating, just like regular bacon.

items: Smokin' Pecan pellets and a smoke tube
Toasted bread, mayo, crisp lettuce and sliced tomato

steps: Cure the beef belly in pastrami brine in the fridge for 10–14 days.
Rinse, soak in fresh water for 1–2 hours, and pat completely dry.
Coat with pastrami rub and let it dry uncovered in the fridge overnight.
On a cool day (ideally under 50°F), light a smoke tube with pecan pellets inside a smoker that's turned off.
Cold smoke the belly for 4–6 hours, keeping the chamber below 50°F.
Chill thoroughly, then slice thin or thick.
Cook the slices in a pan or over a hot grill until the edges crisp. Serve on a BLT or however you like.
notes: Cold-smoked bacon is not cooked. Always cook it before eating.
Firm it up in the freezer for 30 minutes before slicing to get clean, even slices.
Vacuum seal portions. It freezes for months.
review_notes: Cure time, smoke duration, overnight drying and chamber temperature are filled in. Captions confirm beef belly, pastrami brine and rub, cold smoking on a cool rainy day with pecan pellets and a smoke tube, slice and cook to taste, and the BLT.

title: Juicy Smoked Brisket, Start to Finish
summary: My full brisket process: trim, mustard binder, Holy Cow, smoke at 225°F until the bark is locked in, wrap in butcher paper and finish low.
article:
There are too many dried-out, overcooked briskets out there. We can do better. This is my whole process from trim to slice, the same one behind the juiciest briskets on the channel.

## Trim with a purpose

The trim is where a great brisket starts. Take the hard fat down, square off the thin edges that would burn, and round the corners so smoke flows over the meat evenly. Don't throw the trimmings away: I render the fat into tallow and use the lean scraps for burgers and soups. Nothing goes to waste.

## Bark first, then wrap

After a light mustard binder and a good coat of Meat Church Holy Cow, the brisket goes on at 225°F. Be patient. It needs 6–8 hours for the bark to set hard, and the internal temperature should be around 170°F before it gets wrapped. Wrap too early and you trade that crust for a pot roast.

Wrap tight in butcher paper, with a little tallow underneath if the flat looks lean, and bump the smoker to 250°F. From there it's a few more hours until the probe slides in with almost no resistance, usually 200–205°F.

## The rest is half the cook

Leave it wrapped on the counter for 30–60 minutes, then hold it warm. A BBQ blanket, a 150°F oven or a cooler stuffed with towels all work. The longer it holds, the juicier it slices. Stay for the slicing shots in the video. That's the payoff.

items: Meat Church Holy Cow rub (or salt, pepper and garlic)

steps: Trim the brisket: remove hard fat, thin the fat cap to about ¼ inch, and round off any thin edges and corners. Save the trimmings for tallow.
Smear a thin layer of mustard over the whole brisket as a binder, then season heavily with Holy Cow on all sides.
Smoke at 225°F for 6–8 hours, until the bark is very well set and the internal temperature is around 170°F.
Lay out butcher paper, add a spoonful of tallow where the flat will sit if needed, and wrap the brisket tightly.
Raise the smoker to 250°F and continue cooking for a few more hours, until the brisket is probe tender, around 200–205°F.
Rest it wrapped on the counter for 30–60 minutes.
Hold it in a BBQ blanket, a 150°F oven or a towel-lined cooler until you're ready to serve.
Separate the point from the flat, slice the flat against the grain about the thickness of a pencil, and cube or slice the point.
notes: Wrap based on bark, not the clock. If the rub smears, it isn't ready.
Probe the thickest part of the flat. Every brisket finishes at a slightly different temperature.
Leftovers make an incredible brisket ramen.
review_notes: Brisket weight range, fat-cap thickness, slicing guidance, prep time and servings are filled in. Temps, rub and wrap process are from the caption.

title: Smoked & Braised Beef Cheeks
summary: Often called the best bite in BBQ: beef cheeks with a mustard, pepper and Gospel bark, smoked five hours and braised until spoon tender.
article:
Beef cheeks get called the best bite in BBQ for a reason. They're a hard-working muscle loaded with collagen, and when you give them time, they turn rich, silky and almost spoonable. One of you asked if I'd cook them, so I did, and now they're on regular rotation.

The method is the same smoke-then-braise approach that made my pulled chuck roast so popular. First, build bark in open smoke. Then, once it's set, move everything into the broth that's been catching drippings below and let it braise.

## The bark

Mustard as a binder, plenty of black pepper and Meat Church The Gospel. Smoke at 225°F for about five hours, brushing with tallow every so often. Cheeks are small, so keep an eye on them. Once the bark is set, they're ready to braise.

## The braise

Transfer the cheeks into the pan of broth and drippings, cover it, and let them go until probe tender. They'll shrink quite a bit and turn incredibly tender. Spoon some of that braising liquid over the top before serving.

items: 3–4 lb beef cheeks, trimmed of silverskin
1 carton (32 oz) beef or vegetable broth

steps: Set your smoker to 225°F.
Trim any silverskin and hard fat from the cheeks.
Coat the cheeks with a thin layer of mustard, then season with black pepper and The Gospel.
Pour the broth into an aluminum pan and set it below the cheeks to catch drippings.
Smoke for about 5 hours, brushing with tallow occasionally, until the bark is set.
Transfer the cheeks into the pan of broth and cover tightly with foil.
Keep cooking until they are probe tender, usually 205–210°F internal.
Rest for 30 minutes in the liquid, then serve with the braising juices spooned over the top.
notes: Cheeks shrink a lot. Plan on about half the raw weight once cooked.
They're excellent shredded into tacos with a little of the braising liquid.
review_notes: Cheek weight, trimming, braise finish temperature, rest time and servings are filled in. Seasoning, smoke temp/time and braise method are from the caption.

title: Smoked & Braised Pulled Chuck Roast
summary: A 4 lb chuck eye roast smoked low until the bark sets, then braised in broth until it pulls apart. Brisket flavor in about half the time.
article:
Step aside, brisket. This pulled chuck roast is the most tender, flavorful beef I've ever cooked, and it's the cook more of you have asked about than anything else on the channel.

Chuck eye roast comes from right next to the ribeye, so it has the same rich marbling, but it's priced like a weeknight cut. Smoke it like a brisket to build bark, then finish it covered in broth so all that connective tissue melts down. The result shreds with a fork and soaks up the juices like nothing else.

## Why smoke and then braise?

The open smoke at 225°F is all about bark and flavor. I brush the roast with tallow every so often so the surface stays moist and the rub doesn't dry out. A pan of broth sits underneath the whole time catching drippings, so by the time the bark is set, that broth has turned into a smoky beef jus.

Once the bark is where I want it, the roast goes into that pan, gets wrapped tight in foil, and the smoker gets bumped up to 250–275°F. Now it's a braise. You're not chasing a number on the thermometer here, you're waiting for the probe to slide in like butter, usually somewhere around 205–210°F.

## Don't skip the rest

Leave it wrapped for a couple of hours before you pull it. A long rest at around 150°F lets the meat relax and reabsorb the liquid. Pull it right in the pan juices and serve it on buns, in tacos, or straight off the cutting board.

items: Meat Church The Gospel All Purpose rub (or your favorite beef rub)
1 carton (32 oz) beef or vegetable broth

steps: Set your smoker to 225°F.
Season the chuck roast all over with coarse black pepper, then a generous coat of The Gospel.
Pour the broth into an aluminum pan and set it on the grate below the roast to catch the drippings.
Smoke at 225°F for about 5 hours, brushing the roast with melted tallow every hour or so, until the bark is fully set and doesn't smear when you touch it.
Move the roast into the pan of broth and drippings and cover it tightly with aluminum foil.
Raise the smoker to 250–275°F and keep cooking until the roast is probe tender, about 205–210°F internal.
Leave it tightly wrapped and rest for 1–2 hours, ideally in a 150°F oven or a cooler lined with towels.
Pull the meat apart right in the pan so it soaks up the juices. Serve.
notes: Tallow keeps the surface from drying out during the long open smoke. Butter works in a pinch.
Probe tender matters more than any exact temperature. If the probe meets resistance, give it more time.
Save extra pan juice for reheating leftovers so they don't dry out.
review_notes: Prep time and servings are estimates. Broth amount assumed as one 32 oz carton (caption says 'a carton'). Wood type not stated.

title: Wall-to-Wall Medium Rare Ribeye Over Charcoal
summary: Just salt, pepper and a hot charcoal fire for wall-to-wall medium rare. Plus the mistake that cost me a perfect cook, so you don't repeat it.
article:
Some cooks don't need a recipe, just good beef, salt, pepper and a hot fire. These ribeyes came off the charcoal at a perfect medium rare from edge to edge.

## Learn from my mistake

Not every cook goes to plan. On one ribeye cook, I let my coals die down too much and ended up chasing the sear at the expense of the cook. They were still delicious, but not the medium rare I usually enjoy. The lesson: build a bigger fire than you think you need, and make sure the coals are glowing hot before the steaks go on. A hot fire gives you a crust fast, before the inside overcooks.

## Two-zone fire

Bank your coals to one side. Sear directly over the coals, then slide the steaks to the cooler side to finish if they need a minute more. Pull them a few degrees early, since they'll climb while resting.
steps: Season the steaks generously with salt at least 45 minutes before cooking (or the night before), then with pepper right before grilling.
Build a big, two-zone charcoal fire and wait until the coals are glowing hot.
Sear directly over the coals, flipping every minute or so, until a deep crust forms.
Move to the cool side if needed and cook until the center reads 125–128°F for medium rare.
Rest for 5–10 minutes, slice against the grain and serve.
notes: Don't let the coals die down. A weak fire means you'll overcook the inside chasing the crust.
review_notes: Salt and pepper only, charcoal and the 'coals died down' lesson are from your captions. The pull temperature, dry brine timing and two-zone method are filled in.

title: Smoked & Reverse Seared Rack of Lamb with Chimichurri
summary: A contender for best bite of the year: rack of lamb smoked at 225°F to 125°F, rested, seared over ripping hot flames and served with chimichurri.
article:
This rack of lamb was on fire, and it's a serious contender for one of the best things we ate all year.

Smoke it gently at 225°F until it hits 125°F internal, then let it rest for 30 minutes. That rest matters because it lets you sear hard without overcooking the inside. Then it goes over ripping hot flames just long enough to char the fat cap and crust the outside.

I served it with a bright, garlicky chimichurri and roasted veggies. The herbs and vinegar cut right through the richness of the lamb.

items: 2 racks of lamb (frenched, about 1½ lb each)
Kosher salt and coarse black pepper
1 cup packed flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
2 tbsp fresh oregano, chopped (or 2 tsp dried)

steps: Stir together all the chimichurri ingredients and let it sit for at least 30 minutes.
Set your smoker to 225°F. Score the fat cap lightly and season the lamb all over with salt, pepper and garlic.
Smoke until the center reaches 125°F, about 1–1½ hours.
Rest for 30 minutes while you build a ripping hot fire.
Sear over the flames for 1–2 minutes per side, fat side especially, until charred.
Slice between the bones and serve with chimichurri and roasted vegetables.
notes: 125°F before the sear lands you around medium rare.
review_notes: 225°F to 125°F, the 30-minute rest, the flame sear, chimichurri and veggies are from your caption. Seasoning, the chimichurri recipe and rack sizes are filled in.

title: Reverse Seared Picanha
summary: Wall-to-wall medium rare picanha: El Blanco, smoked at 200°F to 130°F, then reverse seared in beef tallow. Plus how to break down a whole top sirloin.
article:
Picanha, the top sirloin cap, is the star of Brazilian steakhouses, and it's one of my favorite cuts to cook on a smoker. Done right, it comes out medium rare from edge to edge with a crisp, rendered fat cap.

## Buy the whole subprimal

I picked up a whole top sirloin subprimal from Costco at $7.99/lb, about $125 total. Breaking it down myself got me more than a dozen sirloin steaks plus a gorgeous picanha, which works out to under $10 a steak. All the trimmings got rendered down for tallow. Watch the breakdown video if you want to try it. It's easier than it looks.

## Smoke low, sear hot

A quick dry brine, a coat of Meat Church El Blanco, and then the smoker at just 200°F. The low temperature is what gives you that even pink all the way through. Pull it at 130°F, rest, then reverse sear in ripping hot beef tallow to build the crust and crisp the fat cap.

Slice against the grain. Picanha's grain changes direction, so check it as you go. Leftovers make an incredible sandwich.
steps: Score the fat cap in a crosshatch without cutting into the meat. Salt it all over and dry brine uncovered in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Set your smoker to 200°F. Season the picanha with El Blanco.
Smoke until the center reads 130°F, about 2–2½ hours.
Rest for 10–15 minutes while you heat a cast iron pan or griddle until it's ripping hot.
Melt the tallow and sear the picanha on all sides, fat cap last, until a deep crust forms.
Slice against the grain and serve.
notes: 130°F off the smoker plus the sear lands you right at medium rare.
Render the subprimal trimmings into tallow and use it for this sear.
review_notes: Picanha weight, fat-cap scoring, dry brine timing and cook duration are filled in. Rub, 200°F to 130°F, tallow sear and subprimal cost are from the captions.

title: Smoked Turkey Breast with Butter Rest
summary: The most underrated BBQ meat: turkey breast with Holy Cow, smoked at 200–250°F to 160°F, then wrapped and rested with butter for an hour. Beats deli meat any day.
article:
Smoked turkey breast might be the most underrated meat in BBQ. It's easy, it's affordable, and it beats store-bought deli meat any day.

I season it with Meat Church Holy Cow and smoke between 200 and 250°F until it hits 160°F internal. Then comes the important part: wrap it in foil with a few pats of butter and let it rest for an hour. The butter melts into the meat as it rests, and carryover heat brings it up to a safe 165°F.

Slice it thick for dinner or thin for the best sandwiches of your life.
steps: Set your smoker to 200–250°F.
Pat the turkey breast dry and season all over with Holy Cow.
Smoke until the thickest part reaches 160°F, about 2–3 hours.
Lay out a sheet of foil, add the butter, place the turkey on top and wrap tightly.
Rest for 1 hour. Carryover heat brings it to 165°F.
Slice against the grain and spoon the buttery juices over the top.
notes: Always confirm 165°F after the rest. Poultry needs to hit it for safety.
review_notes: Rub, temperatures and the butter rest are from your captions. Breast size, cook time and the 165°F carryover note are filled in.

title: Smoked Picanha Sandwich with Horseradish Sauce
summary: Leftover smoked picanha on toasted ciabatta with Havarti, red onion and a sharp horseradish sauce.
article:
Leftover picanha might be even better than the main event. Thin-slice it cold, warm it gently, and pile it on toasted ciabatta with melty Havarti, red onion and a punchy horseradish sauce.

The horseradish sauce takes two minutes and cuts right through the richness of the beef. Make extra, it's great on brisket too.

items: Squeeze of lemon, salt and pepper

steps: Stir together all the horseradish sauce ingredients and refrigerate.
Butter the cut sides of the ciabatta and toast on a griddle or grill until golden.
Warm the sliced picanha in a pan for 30 seconds, then top with Havarti and cover until melted.
Spread horseradish sauce on the bread, pile on the beef and cheese, add red onion and serve.
review_notes: Horseradish sauce recipe and all quantities are filled in. Components (ciabatta, horseradish sauce, Havarti, red onion) are from the caption.

title: Leftover Brisket Ramen
summary: Ramen plus brisket equals heaven. My favorite way to use up leftover smoked brisket.
article:
Ramen and brisket might be my favorite combo, and it's the best use of leftovers I know. The smoky, fatty brisket melts into the broth and turns a simple bowl of noodles into something special.

Use fatty point slices if you have them. Warm them in the broth just long enough to heat through so they stay tender.

items: 2 cloves garlic, grated, and 1 tsp grated ginger
Sliced scallions, sesame seeds and chili oil, to finish

steps: Simmer the broth with soy sauce, miso, garlic and ginger for 10 minutes.
Cook the noodles according to the package and divide between bowls.
Warm the brisket slices in the simmering broth for 1–2 minutes.
Ladle the broth over the noodles, top with brisket, eggs, scallions, sesame seeds and chili oil.
notes: Add any leftover brisket jus to the broth for even more flavor.
review_notes: The caption only says 'Ramen + Brisket = Heaven'. The broth and toppings are a standard recipe I filled in.

title: Pickle Juice Brined Wings
summary: Wings brined in pickle juice and brown sugar, tossed in Kinder's garlic butter and charred over an open flame. The weekend wing that never fails.
article:
These have quickly become an absolute favorite for everyone here. The pickle juice brine never fails. It seasons the wings all the way through, keeps them juicy, and gives them a subtle tangy flavor that's hard to place but impossible to stop eating.

## The brine

It's simple: ¾ cup pickle juice and ½ cup brown sugar for 3 lb of wings. Brine for 2–4 hours, rinse and pat completely dry.

## Over the fire

Toss them with a little olive oil and your favorite seasoning (I used Kinder's garlic butter) and char them over an open flame on the Millscale Yakitori. Cook until they hit at least 165°F. Wings are forgiving, and they get even better around 175–185°F as the fat renders.

items: Kinder's Garlic Butter seasoning (or your favorite)

steps: Whisk the pickle juice and brown sugar until the sugar dissolves.
Add the wings, toss to coat, and refrigerate for 2–4 hours.
Rinse the wings and pat them completely dry.
Toss with olive oil and season generously.
Grill over a hot open flame, turning often, until charred and at least 165°F internal.
Rest for a few minutes and serve.
notes: Don't brine longer than 4 hours. The acid starts to change the texture.
review_notes: Recipe amounts and method are from your caption. The 175–185°F suggestion and cook time are filled in.

title: Beef Belly Pastrami Burnt Ends
summary: Porter Road beef belly brined for two weeks, crusted in pastrami rub, cubed and smoked into ruby red bites of pure flavor.
article:
Pastrami flavor in a burnt-end package. I picked up some gorgeous beef belly from Porter Road, the cut that beef bacon comes from, and gave it the full pastrami treatment.

## Why beef belly?

Beef belly is loaded with fat, like the point of a brisket but even richer. That fat renders down into tender, juicy bites that hold up to a heavy cure and a thick pepper crust.

## The process

The belly brined for about two weeks in my pastrami brine, then got a heavy coat of my homemade pastrami rub. Smoke it until the bark sets, cube it, and finish in a pan until the cubes are tender. They come out ruby red inside with a peppery crust on every side.

items: 2 tbsp beef tallow or butter, for the pan

steps: Submerge the beef belly in pastrami brine and refrigerate for about 2 weeks.
Rinse, soak in fresh water for 1–2 hours, and pat dry.
Coat heavily with pastrami rub.
Smoke at 250°F until the bark is set, about 4–5 hours.
Cut into 1½-inch cubes, toss in a pan with tallow, and cover with foil.
Return to the smoker until the cubes are probe tender, 1–2 more hours.
Rest uncovered for 10 minutes and serve.
notes: Beef belly is thinner than brisket, so it doesn't need quite as long in the brine.
review_notes: Smoker temperature, cube and pan finish, and times are filled in. Caption confirms Porter Road beef belly, about 2 weeks of brine, homemade pastrami rub and smoked until tender.

title: Simple Smoked Cream Cheese
summary: A block of cream cheese, scored, seasoned with Texas Sugar, Honey Hog and everything bagel, and smoked for two hours. The easiest crowd-pleaser there is.
article:
Smoked cream cheese might be the easiest crowd-pleaser in BBQ. Score it, season it, smoke it for a couple of hours, and watch it disappear.

My favorite seasonings are Meat Church Texas Sugar, Meat Church Honey Hog and some everything bagel seasoning, either all together or one per block if you're making a few. Scoring the top in a crosshatch pattern gives the seasoning and smoke more places to settle and creates those golden ridges.

Serve it warm with bagel chips, crackers, a drizzle of honey or a spoonful of pepper jelly or jam.

items: Bagel chips, crackers, honey or jam, for serving

steps: Set your smoker to 225°F.
Unwrap the cream cheese onto a small pan and score the top in a crosshatch pattern about ¼ inch deep.
Season all sides generously with your rubs and everything bagel seasoning.
Smoke for about 2 hours, until the top is golden and the ridges have opened up.
Serve warm with bagel chips, honey or jam.
notes: Use a disposable pan or foil boat. It gets soft and is hard to move otherwise.
review_notes: Seasonings, temperature and time are from your caption. The crosshatch scoring is from the video. Servings are an estimate.

title: Bacon-Wrapped Smoked Jalapeño Poppers
summary: The most addictive thing I've ever smoked: jalapeños stuffed with a cheddar and Honey Hog cream cheese filling, wrapped in bacon and smoked at 275°F until crispy.
article:
These jalapeño poppers have been the biggest hit at any party I've brought them to. Nothing else even comes close. They're one of the most addictive things I've ever smoked.

## Make the filling your own

Start with softened cream cheese and mix in whatever you like. I went with shredded cheddar and Meat Church Honey Hog for a little sweetness. Halve the jalapeños, scrape out the seeds and ribs, and pack them full.

## Bacon and heat

Wrap each half in a slice of bacon (thin-cut wraps and crisps more easily), season the outside, and smoke at 275°F for about an hour and a half, until the bacon is nice and crispy. Let them cool for a few minutes before serving, because the filling is molten.

items: 1 tbsp Meat Church Honey Hog rub, plus more for dusting

steps: Set your smoker to 275°F.
Mix the cream cheese, cheddar and Honey Hog until smooth.
Fill each jalapeño half with the cream cheese mixture.
Wrap each one in a half slice of bacon, tucking the ends underneath.
Dust lightly with more Honey Hog and arrange on a rack or popper tray.
Smoke for about 1½ hours, until the bacon is nice and crispy.
Rest for 5 minutes before serving.
notes: Leave a few ribs in if you like heat. Scrape them clean if you don't.
A jalapeño rack keeps them upright so the filling doesn't run out.
review_notes: Filling, 275°F and 1.5 hours are from your caption. Quantities (12 jalapeños, cream cheese and cheddar amounts) are filled in.

title: How to Render Beef Tallow from Brisket Trimmings
summary: Don't toss your brisket trimmings. Render the fat into liquid gold for searing, wrapping and brushing, and use the lean scraps for burgers.
article:
Every time I post a brisket trim, someone asks what to do with all those trimmings. Make tallow! I always render the leftover beef fat into tallow and use the trimmed meat in soups, hamburgers and more.

Tallow comes up again and again in my cooks. I brush it on chuck roasts and beef cheeks, add it to the butcher paper when wrapping brisket, and use it to sear picanha. Once you have a jar in the fridge, you'll use it constantly.

## Low and slow, again

Cut the fat into small pieces or grind it, and melt it gently. Low heat is what keeps the tallow clean and mild instead of brown and beefy-burnt. Strain it through a coffee filter and you end up with clear, golden fat that sets up firm and white in the fridge.

items: 2–4 lb beef fat trimmings (from brisket or other cuts)

steps: Separate any lean meat from the trimmings and save it for burgers or soup.
Cut the fat into small cubes, or pulse it in a food processor or grinder.
Put the fat and water in a heavy pot or a pan in a 250°F smoker.
Render on low heat for 2–4 hours, stirring occasionally, until the solids are small, crisp and golden.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer lined with a coffee filter into clean jars.
Cool, then cover and refrigerate. It keeps for months.
notes: Rendering in the smoker gives you smoked tallow, which is great for searing steaks.
The water just keeps the fat from scorching before it starts to melt. It cooks off.
review_notes: The caption only says to render the trimmings into tallow and use the meat for soups and burgers. The rendering method and amounts are standard values I filled in. The video shows straining through a coffee filter into a mason jar.

title: Smoked & Braised Oxtails with Parmesan Polenta
summary: Oxtails smoked until the bark sets, then braised in red wine, stock and mirepoix until fork tender. Served over parmesan polenta with the reduced braise as a sauce.
article:
I hadn't been this excited for a cook in a while. I'd never even eaten oxtails before, let alone cooked them. This turned into one of the most technical and fun cooks I've done so far, and it was a huge hit.

## Smoke first

The oxtails get a simple seasoning of black pepper and Meat Church El Blanco, then go into the smoker for about four hours until the bark is nicely set. Oxtails are mostly bone, fat and collagen, so that smoky crust gives the finished braise a lot of depth.

## Build the braise under the meat

While the oxtails smoke, make the braising liquid: beef stock, red wine, a mirepoix of onion, carrot and celery, tomato paste, herbs and garlic. I set the pan of liquid right under the oxtails so it heats up and catches the drippings while they finish smoking. When the bark is ready, the whole rack goes into the pan, covered tight, for about three more hours until fork tender.

## Finish like a restaurant

Pull the oxtails, strain and reduce the braising liquid until it coats a spoon, and serve over creamy parmesan polenta with asparagus. Spoon the sauce over everything.

items: Meat Church El Blanco rub (or salt and garlic)
A few sprigs fresh thyme and rosemary, 2 bay leaves

steps: Set your smoker to 250°F. Season the oxtails with black pepper and El Blanco.
Smoke for about 4 hours, until the bark is well set.
Meanwhile, sauté the onion, carrot and celery in a little oil until soft. Stir in the tomato paste and garlic and cook for 2 minutes.
Add the red wine and stock, plus the herbs, and transfer to a deep aluminum or cast iron pan.
Set the pan of braising liquid under the oxtails for the last hour of smoking so it heats up and catches the drippings.
Move the oxtails into the liquid, cover tightly with foil, and braise for about 3 hours, until fork tender.
Remove the oxtails. Strain the liquid, skim the fat, and simmer until it reduces to a glossy sauce.
Serve the oxtails over parmesan polenta with asparagus and plenty of sauce.
notes: The braise is just as good the next day. Chill it overnight and lift off the solid fat before reheating.
Use a red wine you'd actually drink. It reduces down and becomes the backbone of the sauce.
review_notes: Smoker temperature and all braise quantities are filled in; the caption lists the braise ingredients but not amounts. Smoke and braise times, seasoning and serving are from the caption.

title: Smoked & Braised Short Ribs in Red Wine
summary: The oxtail method applied to beef short ribs: Holy Cow, six hours of smoke at 225°F, then a red wine braise. Served over parmesan polenta.
article:
I loved the oxtail cook so much that I decided to try short ribs the exact same way. Same idea, meatier result.

The short ribs get rubbed with Meat Church Holy Cow and smoked at 225°F for around six hours to build a deep bark. Then they finish covered in a red wine reduction until they're falling off the bone. It's fancy enough for a dinner party, but most of the work is just waiting.

Serve them over parmesan polenta and spoon the reduced braise over the top.

items: 4–5 lb bone-in beef short ribs (English cut)
1 onion, 2 carrots and 2 celery stalks, diced

steps: Set your smoker to 225°F. Season the short ribs heavily with Holy Cow.
Smoke for about 6 hours, until the bark is well set.
While they smoke, sauté the vegetables, stir in the tomato paste and garlic, then add the wine, stock and herbs. Simmer for 10 minutes.
Move the ribs into a pan with the braising liquid, cover tightly, and cook at 275°F until fork tender, 2–3 hours.
Remove the ribs, strain and reduce the liquid to a sauce, and serve over polenta.
notes: Leave the bones in. They add body to the braise and hold the meat together.
review_notes: Braise ingredients, amounts, braise temperature and time are filled in, modeled on the oxtail cook. Rub, 225°F for about 6 hours, red wine reduction and polenta are from the caption.

title: Smoked Bulgogi Beef Jerky
summary: Thin-sliced bulgogi ribeye marinated overnight in Bachan's, soy and chili flakes, then smoked low for about five hours.
article:
The secret to this jerky is the meat. I buy thin-sliced frozen bulgogi ribeye from my local Korean market. It's relatively cheap for such high-quality meat, and it comes sliced to the perfect thickness, so there's no partially freezing and slicing a roast yourself.

## The marinade

Bachan's Japanese barbecue sauce does most of the work. I thin it with extra soy sauce and a little water and add red pepper flakes for heat. The ribeye marinates overnight.

## Low and slow

Lay the slices flat on racks and smoke at 160–170°F for about five hours, until the jerky bends and cracks but doesn't snap. Let it cool completely before storing.

items: 2 lb thin-sliced bulgogi ribeye (from a Korean market)

steps: Whisk together the Bachan's, soy sauce, water and red pepper flakes.
Separate the ribeye slices, add them to the marinade, and refrigerate overnight.
Drain and pat the slices dry, then lay them flat on wire racks without overlapping.
Smoke at 160–170°F for about 5 hours, until the jerky bends and cracks but doesn't snap.
Cool completely on the racks before storing in an airtight jar or bag.
notes: For extra safety, USDA recommends the meat reach 160°F. Many jerky makers start the smoker hotter (around 200°F) for the first 30 minutes, then drop it.
Keeps for weeks in an airtight jar and even longer in the fridge.
review_notes: Marinade amounts and meat weight are filled in. Your caption says it 'lasts months in a jar at room temp'. I softened that to weeks in a jar and longer in the fridge, and added the USDA 160°F safety note.

title: Smoked Beef Short Ribs
summary: Dino-style beef short ribs with Holy Cow, smoked at 250°F until probe tender. Minimal trim, minimal fuss.
article:
Beef short ribs are about as simple as smoked meat gets: minimal trim, apply your rub, and smoke them at 250°F until they're probe tender. It doesn't get much more straightforward than that.

My first try wasn't quite up to my standards. The meat was plenty tender, but not as juicy as I'd hoped. It was still a delicious failure, and the neighbors loved them. The second round nailed it.

## Keep it simple

I used Meat Church Holy Cow and Bear Mountain pellets. Leave the fat cap mostly alone, just remove the thick membrane on top and any loose bits. Short ribs carry so much intramuscular fat that they baste themselves.

## Know when they're done

Don't pull them on time or temperature alone. Probe between the bones. When it slides in with no resistance, usually somewhere past 200°F, they're ready. Pull them too early and they'll be tough. Rest them at least 30 minutes before slicing between the bones.

items: 1 rack beef plate short ribs (3–4 bones, 4–5 lb)
Yellow mustard or oil, as a binder (optional)

steps: Set your smoker to 250°F.
Do a minimal trim: remove the tough membrane on the meat side and any loose fat.
Apply a light binder if you like, then season all sides generously with Holy Cow.
Smoke at 250°F until probe tender between the bones, around 200–205°F internal. Expect 7–9 hours.
Spritz occasionally after the first 3 hours if the edges look dry.
Rest for at least 30 minutes, then slice between the bones and serve.
notes: If your first rack comes out tender but dry, try spritzing more and resting longer in a warm cooler.
Bear Mountain pellets were my pick here. Oak or hickory blends work great with beef.
review_notes: Rib size, cook duration, finish temperature, spritz step and rest time are filled in. Rub, pellets and 250°F to probe tender are from the caption.

title: No-Wrap St. Louis Ribs
summary: St. Louis ribs with Meat Church Gospel, spritzed with apple cider vinegar and apple juice, glazed with Whomp sauce and smoked about five hours, no wrap.
article:
These St. Louis ribs never fail to impress. The Gospel rub plus Meat Mitch's Whomp sauce is an amazing combination, and the ribs have that perfect deep mahogany color.

## No wrap needed

A lot of people ask how to get a tender bite without wrapping. You can get a great tender bite without sacrificing your bark just by letting them go a little longer. Skip the foil, trust the spritz, and give them the time they need. In the slicing video, the last rack got a little extra heat and you can see it starting to fall apart on its own.

## The process

A mustard binder and a full coat of Meat Church The Gospel. Spritz with a 50/50 mix of apple cider vinegar and apple juice once the bark starts to set. Sauce with Whomp near the end so it tightens up into a glaze, not a sticky mess. All in, it's about five hours.

items: 2 racks St. Louis-cut pork spare ribs
½ cup apple cider vinegar plus ½ cup apple juice, in a spray bottle

steps: Set your smoker to 250°F.
Remove the membrane from the back of each rack and trim any loose flaps.
Coat with a thin layer of mustard, then season generously with The Gospel on both sides.
Smoke bone side down. After about 2 hours, once the bark has set, spritz every 45 minutes with the vinegar and apple juice mix.
Around the 4½-hour mark, brush on a layer of Whomp sauce and let it set for 20–30 minutes.
The ribs are done when they bend and crack on the surface when lifted from one end, and a probe slides between the bones easily. Expect about 5 hours total.
Rest for 10 minutes and slice between the bones.
notes: For a more fall-apart bite without wrapping, just let them go a little longer.
Sauce late. Sugar burns if it goes on too early.
review_notes: Rub, spritz, sauce, about 5 hours and no wrap are from your captions. The 250°F smoker temperature, spritz timing, sauce timing and doneness test are filled in.

title: Miso-Rubbed Smoked & Flame-Grilled Pork Shoulder
summary: An experiment that worked: miso paste as a binder, Gospel rub, smoked to 170°F, thin sliced and charred over a blazing yakitori grill.
article:
This little experiment on a pork shoulder turned out amazing. Instead of mustard, I used miso paste as the binder. It adds a deep, savory, slightly funky flavor and caramelizes beautifully.

## Smoked and grilled

I rubbed it with miso and Meat Church The Gospel and smoked it until about 170°F internal. That's well short of pulled pork temperature, so the meat holds together and you can slice it. Then I sliced it thin and seared the slices over a ripping hot fire on my Millscale Yakitori grill.

The result is tender, smoky slices with crispy, charred edges and a deep, savory flavor. It's somewhere between char siu and Korean BBQ.

items: 3–4 tbsp white or yellow miso paste

steps: Set your smoker to 250°F.
Smear the miso paste over the whole shoulder as a binder, then season with The Gospel.
Smoke until the internal temperature is about 170°F.
Rest for 20 minutes, then slice thin, about ⅓ inch.
Build a hot charcoal fire in a yakitori-style or close-to-the-coals grill.
Sear the slices for 30–60 seconds per side, until charred at the edges. Serve right away.
notes: Pork is safe at 145°F, so slicing at 170°F is fully cooked. The final sear is for texture and char.
review_notes: Binder, rub, about 170°F, thin slicing and the yakitori sear are from your captions. Smoker temperature, miso amount, slice thickness and timing are filled in.

title: Zero-Effort Hatch Chile Pulled Pork
summary: Costco's seasonal Hatch chile marinated pork shoulder, smoked for bark, finished covered and pulled when probe tender. No extra seasoning needed.
article:
I can't believe it took me this long to post a pulled pork video. This was a Hatch chile marinated pork shoulder I grabbed from Costco during the season and deep froze for later. It was a zero-effort cook with amazing results.

The marinade already has everything it needs, so skip the extra seasoning. Toss it on the smoker until you get a good bark, transfer it to a covered pan to finish, and pull it when it's probe tender.

See one of these at Costco this summer? Grab two and freeze one.

items: 1 Costco Hatch chile marinated pork shoulder (about 8 lb), thawed
Buns, tortillas and slaw, for serving

steps: Thaw the shoulder in the fridge for 2–3 days if frozen.
Set your smoker to 250°F.
Smoke the shoulder straight from the package, no extra seasoning, until a good bark forms, around 165–170°F internal.
Transfer to a pan, pour in any juices from the package, and cover tightly with foil.
Continue cooking until probe tender, around 200–205°F.
Rest covered for at least 1 hour, then pull and toss with the pan juices.
review_notes: Process is from your caption. Smoker temperature, internal temperatures, weight and timing are filled in.

title: New York Kosher Brisket Pastrami
summary: Kosher briskets brought home from New York, cured for just over two weeks and smoked into the best pastrami I've made.
article:
I was lucky enough to be traveling to New York and took the chance to pick up a few kosher briskets. If you're going to make pastrami, why not start where pastrami lives?

Kosher beef goes through a salting process during koshering, so it starts out lightly seasoned. That's worth knowing before you build the brine. Some people cut back the salt a little for kosher meat, and a fry test after the soak is the best way to check.

## The wait is the hard part

These brined for a little over two weeks. Then came the usual routine: rinse, soak, a heavy rub, and into the smoker until the bark was set. I wrapped them once they were almost ready and finished low until probe tender.

The slicing teaser says it all. Look at that color.

items: Pastrami brine (same as my Smoked Brisket Pastrami; consider slightly less salt for kosher beef)

steps: Make the pastrami brine and chill it completely.
Submerge the brisket and cure in the fridge for about 2 weeks, flipping every few days.
Rinse and soak in fresh water for 2–4 hours. Fry a test slice to check the salt.
Pat dry and apply a heavy coat of pastrami rub.
Smoke at 225–250°F until the bark is set, then wrap.
Continue until probe tender, rest for at least an hour, and slice thin.
notes: The full brine and rub are in the Smoked Brisket Pastrami and Pastrami Rub posts.
review_notes: The kosher salt note and the cook steps follow the main pastrami method. Captions confirm only the kosher briskets from NY, about 2 weeks of brine, wrapping and slicing.

title: Smoked & Seared Pork Loin
summary: Pork loin with Meat Church Gospel and Texas Sugar, smoked at 225°F to 140°F and seared in a 550°F oven for two minutes. Juicy every time.
article:
Pork loin gets a bad reputation for being dry, but it doesn't have to be. Pull it at the right temperature and it's one of the juiciest, most affordable cuts you can smoke.

My first one went a little past where I like it and was still plenty juicy. This version nails it: Meat Church The Gospel and Texas Sugar, smoked at 225°F until 140°F internal, then seared in a 550°F oven for just two minutes to crisp up the crust.

## Smoke it ahead

Fun fact: one of the loins in my videos was smoked two months earlier and vacuum sealed. I brought it back to life with a sous vide bath and a quick trip under the broiler, and it tasted freshly cooked. Served with mashed potatoes and asparagus, who could complain?
steps: Set your smoker to 225°F.
Trim any silverskin and coat the loin with a thin layer of mustard.
Season all over with The Gospel, then a layer of Texas Sugar.
Smoke until the center reaches 140°F, about 2½–3 hours.
Sear in a 550°F oven (or over a hot grill) for about 2 minutes to crisp the crust.
Rest for 10 minutes. Carryover heat takes it to the USDA-safe 145°F. Slice and serve.
notes: Make ahead: vacuum seal the cooled loin and freeze. Reheat in a 140°F sous vide bath, then broil to crisp.
review_notes: Rubs, 225°F to 140°F and the 550°F sear for 2 minutes are from your caption. The sous vide reheat is from a separate video. Loin weight, mustard binder and cook duration are filled in.

title: Galbi (Korean Grilled Short Ribs)
summary: A family favorite weeknight cook: thin flanken-cut short ribs in a sweet soy, pear and garlic marinade, grilled hot and fast over charcoal.
article:
Galbi is a family favorite here and an easy weeknight win. Flanken-cut short ribs are sliced thin across the bones, so they marinate quickly and cook in minutes over a hot fire.

I grill some the usual marinated way and some with just salt and pepper, so you can taste the beef on its own. Both are great. The marinated ones caramelize into sweet, savory, charred edges that are hard to stop eating.

The classic marinade uses grated Asian pear. Its enzymes help tenderize the meat and add a gentle sweetness.

items: 3 lb flanken-cut beef short ribs (about ½ inch thick)
Sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, to finish

steps: Rinse the short ribs briefly to remove any bone fragments and pat dry.
Mix all the marinade ingredients, add the ribs, and refrigerate for 4 hours or overnight.
Build a hot charcoal fire.
Grill the ribs for 2–3 minutes per side, until caramelized and charred at the edges.
Cut between the bones with kitchen shears, top with scallions and sesame seeds, and serve with rice.
notes: For the plain version, just salt and pepper the ribs and grill the same way.
review_notes: Captions mention galbi as a family favorite, grilled both marinated and with salt and pepper. The marinade is a standard galbi recipe I filled in. Please replace it with your family's version if it differs.

title: Grilled Buffalo Chicken Lettuce Wraps
summary: A lighter meal-prep break from all the red meat: buffalo-marinated chicken grilled over coals, chopped and piled into lettuce cups with slaw and ranch.
article:
Every once in a while, I need a break from all the BBQ red meat. These buffalo chicken lettuce wraps came out of a weekend of meal prep, and they're simple, healthy and packed with flavor.

The chicken goes into buffalo sauce before grilling, then gets chopped and tossed in a little more sauce. Pile it into crisp lettuce cups with shredded red and green cabbage, scallions and a drizzle of ranch or blue cheese.

items: 2 lb boneless skinless chicken breasts, butterflied or pounded thin
1 head butter or iceberg lettuce, leaves separated

steps: Toss the chicken with half the buffalo sauce and the olive oil and marinate for 30 minutes.
Grill over medium-high heat until it reaches 165°F, about 4–5 minutes per side.
Rest for 5 minutes, then chop and toss with the remaining buffalo sauce.
Fill the lettuce cups with cabbage, buffalo chicken, scallions and a drizzle of dressing.
notes: Store the chicken and toppings separately for meal prep, and assemble right before eating.
review_notes: The caption only names the dish and mentions meal prep. Amounts and steps are filled in, with the toppings taken from what the video shows.

title: My Pastrami Rub
summary: The pastrami rub so many of you asked for: a heavy, coarse crust of black pepper and coriander with a little garlic, onion and paprika.
article:
This is the rub a lot of you keep asking for. Pastrami bark is all about coarse black pepper and coriander. That pairing is what makes pastrami taste like pastrami, and the rest is supporting cast.

Crack the pepper and coriander yourself if you can. Pre-ground spices turn to dust and won't give you that craggy, crunchy crust.

Use it heavy. Pastrami should be fully coated, almost black once it's smoked. This makes enough for one big brisket with a little left over for beef belly or bacon.

items: ¼ cup coarse black pepper (16 mesh)

steps: Toast the coriander and mustard seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, then let them cool.
Crack them coarsely in a spice grinder or with the bottom of a pan.
Mix everything together in a bowl.
Apply heavily to a cured, rinsed and dried brisket or beef belly.
notes: No salt in this rub, because the meat is already cured.
Stores for months in an airtight jar.
review_notes: The video shows the rub being mixed, but the caption gives no amounts. This is a standard pepper-and-coriander ratio I filled in. Please replace it with your exact recipe.

title: Homemade Smoked Brisket Pastrami
summary: The cook that started it all: brisket wet-cured for up to two weeks, crusted in pepper and coriander, smoked at 225–250°F and wrapped until probe tender.
article:
Pastrami is the cook that started my love affair with BBQ, and it's still the one I'm proudest of. Store-bought doesn't come close. You need patience, since the brine takes up to two weeks, but the hands-on work is easy.

## The brine does the heavy lifting

A pastrami brine is a wet cure: water, salt, sugar, pickling spices and pink curing salt. The curing salt gives pastrami its ruby red color and cured flavor, and it's what makes the long brine safe. My first cook brined for 12 days. For the monster 23 lb packer, I cut off the front of the flat because it wouldn't fit in my brine bin, cooked that after 9 days, and let the rest go a full two weeks. The thicker the meat, the longer it needs for the cure to reach the center.

## Rub and smoke

After the brine, rinse the brisket and soak it in fresh water for a few hours to pull out some of the surface salt. Then coat it in a heavy pepper and coriander rub (the recipe is in its own post). Smoke at 225–250°F, overnight for a big one, until the bark sets, then wrap and finish until probe tender.

On a really thick brisket I've debated going no-wrap, but wrapping keeps pastrami juicy and makes it slice beautifully.

## How to eat it

Reuben sandwich, in an omelet, or plain with pickles. Tell me your favorite. Slice it thin against the grain, and steam leftovers to reheat so they stay tender.

items: 4 tsp Prague Powder #1 (pink curing salt), or the amount your cure's label specifies for an immersion brine
1 whole packer brisket (12–16 lb), or a flat
DKCraftBBQ pastrami rub: coarse black pepper and coriander (see the pastrami rub recipe)

steps: Heat about a quarter of the water with the salt, sugar, pickling spice and garlic until dissolved. Add the rest of the water cold, cool completely, then stir in the curing salt.
Trim the brisket of hard fat and submerge it fully in the brine in a food-safe container. Weigh it down if it floats.
Refrigerate for 9–14 days depending on thickness, flipping it every couple of days.
Remove the brisket, rinse well, and soak in fresh cold water for 2–4 hours, changing the water once. This pulls out excess salt.
Pat dry and coat heavily on all sides with pastrami rub.
Smoke at 225–250°F until the bark is set and the internal temperature is around 165–170°F.
Wrap in butcher paper or foil and continue until probe tender, about 200–203°F.
Rest wrapped for at least an hour, then slice thin against the grain.
notes: Always follow the dosage on your curing salt package. Curing salt is not optional and not interchangeable with table salt.
Fry a small slice after the soak. If it's too salty, soak a few more hours.
Steam leftover slices for a few minutes to reheat. They come back just like deli pastrami.
review_notes: Brine recipe and cure amount are a standard formula I filled in. Please check them against your actual brine. Soak step, wrap and finish temperatures, and servings are also filled in. Brine times (9, 12, 14 days), 225–250°F and wrapped to probe tender are from the captions.

title: Flame-Grilled Skirt Steak Fajitas
summary: Marinated skirt steak seared over live fire on the yakitori grill, sliced thin over charred peppers and onions.
article:
Skirt steak was made for live fire. It's thin, loaded with beefy flavor, and it cooks in minutes over a screaming hot fire. I like it on the Millscale Yakitori, where the steak sits right over the coals.

A quick citrus, garlic and spice marinade adds plenty of flavor without masking the beef. Grill the peppers and onions alongside, slice the steak thin against the grain, and pile everything onto warm tortillas.

items: Cilantro, lime wedges, salsa and guacamole

steps: Whisk the marinade ingredients together, add the skirt steak, and refrigerate for 2–6 hours.
Build a very hot charcoal fire.
Grill the peppers and onions in a grill basket until softened and charred.
Pat the steak dry and grill directly over the coals for 2–3 minutes per side, until it reaches 130–135°F.
Rest for 5 minutes, then slice thin against the grain.
Serve with the peppers and onions on warm tortillas with your favorite toppings.
notes: Skirt steak has a long, obvious grain. Cut it into 5–6 inch sections first, then slice each one across the grain.
review_notes: Captions only say flame-grilled skirt steak fajitas on the Millscale Yakitori. The marinade, temperatures and timing are a standard recipe I filled in.

title: Smoked Prime Rib Roast
summary: A bone-in rib roast smoked low and finished with a hard sear. Under, over or perfect? You be the judge.
article:
My first time making a smoked rib roast, and the slicing video got a lot of you arguing in the comments: under, over or perfect?

The smoker is made for this cut. Low heat cooks it evenly from edge to edge, the smoke adds a layer you'll never get from an oven, and a quick high-heat finish brings back the crust. Season it simply and let the beef shine.

## Pull it early

The one rule: pull it before you think you should. A big roast keeps climbing while it rests. For medium rare, take it off the smoker around 120–125°F, then sear it and let it rest.

items: 1 bone-in standing rib roast (3–4 bones, 7–9 lb)
2 tbsp beef tallow or butter, for searing

steps: The night before, season the roast all over with salt and refrigerate it uncovered on a rack.
Set your smoker to 225°F. Season the roast with black pepper and garlic.
Smoke bone side down until the center reaches 120–125°F for medium rare, about 3½–4½ hours.
Rest for 20 minutes while you get a grill or oven ripping hot (500°F+).
Rub with tallow or butter and sear for a few minutes per side, until a deep crust forms.
Slice off the bones, then slice the roast across the grain and serve.
notes: Cook to temperature, not time. Always use a probe thermometer for this cut.
review_notes: The captions only say 'first time making smoked rib roast'. The seasoning, temperatures, times and sear are a standard method I filled in. Please check them against what you actually did.

title: Pork Belly Burnt Ends
summary: Candy-like cubes of smoked pork belly seasoned with Meat Church rubs, finished in butter, honey and sauce until sticky.
article:
Pork belly burnt ends are BBQ candy. Cubes of fatty belly get a heavy coat of Meat Church rub and smoke until the bark sets. Then they finish in a pan with butter, brown sugar, honey and sauce until they turn sticky, glossy and melt-in-your-mouth tender.

Cut them evenly so they cook at the same rate, and give them room on the grate so smoke can reach every side.

items: 3–4 lb skinless pork belly, cut into 1½-inch cubes
Meat Church Honey Hog rub (or your favorite pork rub)

steps: Set your smoker to 250°F.
Season the pork belly cubes generously on all sides.
Smoke on a rack for about 3 hours, until the bark is set and they're a deep mahogany color.
Move them to a pan and add the butter, brown sugar, honey and sauce. Toss to coat, then cover with foil.
Cook for another 1–1½ hours, until probe tender.
Uncover, stir, and cook for 10–15 more minutes so the sauce tightens into a glaze.
review_notes: The caption only says 'Pork belly burnt ends with Meat Church rubs.' The specific rub, temperatures, times and glaze are a standard method I filled in.
